newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to seek support for vision of safer Europe.
newsitem.headline: Russia to seek support for vision of safer Europe.

text.p: Russia will try to get Europe to back its vision of a safer continent at a security summit next week, but failure could complicate important arms talks and toughen its opposition to NATO's expansion plans.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin heads a Russian delegation which has pinned high hopes on the Lisbon summit, gathering leaders of the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) on Monday and Tuesday.
Russia wants to persuade its sceptical Western partners that the OSCE should have a leading role in security matters in Europe and act as a counterbalance to NATO.
"We are going to Lisbon in an optimistic mood," Vsevolod Sukhov, deputy head of the Russian foreign ministry's European cooperation department, told Reuters in an interview.
"We are optimistic that our ideas will be adequately reflected in documents adopted at the summit and appeal to our OSCE partners to be realistic in their approach."
Moscow wants to create a pan-European security system which is free of blocs and divisions, guarantees equal security to all participants and controls arms levels on the continent.
It says such proposals should be adopted in Lisbon with a view to having a treaty ready for signing at the OSCE's next summit in 1998. But most other countries have reacted coolly.

Small states are wary of proposals for Europe to be guided by a "steering group" modelled on the United Nations Security Council. Most countries say NATO, of which Moscow is not a member, must play the leading role in security affairs.
A foreign policy expert close to the Kremlin said he doubted Chernomyrdin or Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov would make any important new proposals in Lisbon.
"There are no major new elements," said Sergei Karaganov, an analyst at Moscow's independent Institute of Europe.
Asked what were the chances of Russia winning Western support for its proposals, he said: "Very little".

The Russian delegation could leave Lisbon disappointed, a prospect which does not augur well for the debate on NATO's plans to expand to include countries of central and eastern Europe -- Moscow's former partners in the defunct Warsaw Pact.
Russia opposes such plans and is working hard to ensure the planned political declaration in Lisbon is free of any wording which could be interpreted as support for enlargement.
Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, in Belarus on Wednesday to witness the withdrawal of the last Soviet nuclear missiles back on to Russian territory, strongly underlined that opposition.

"We are moving away missiles but NATO may already be planning to expand its arsenal, including the nuclear one, closer to the territory of Belarus and Russia," he said. "We are resolutely, definitely against NATO expansion eastwards."

First Deputy Foreign Minister Igor Ivanov told the Krasnaya Zvyezda newspaper last week that Russia was doing all it could through diplomacy to soften the likely blow of NATO expansion. He made clear Moscow would respond if enlargement went ahead.
"All this would force us to correct our plans for military reform," he said, giving no details.

Moscow is also demanding clear progress in Lisbon on revision of the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty, which sets levels on conventional weapons and limits where they can be placed. It wants an agreement reached in 18 months.

"We hope our partners will have the common sense to take the Russian position as its basis (for agreement on CFE)," Ivanov said. "If not, we must be ready to use other politico-military and diplomatic means of actions to make Russia's voice heard."

A foreign ministry spokesman said last week that decisions on arms control issues in Lisbon must be "substantive" and that developments on CFE would "determine our approach to other aspects of relations with a number of member states".
